summary: Announces that two new Telnet options have been specified: Negotiate About Output Line Width (NAOL) and Negotiate About Output Page Size (NAOP). It names the NIC documents and the people who prepared them and put them on-line.

eli5.summary: Two new settings were added to the remote-login tool, so computers can agree on how wide and how tall the screen is.

subtitle: Two new options let Telnet sessions agree on display size

tldr.problem: When a user connected via Telnet from a remote terminal to a network host, neither side knew the width and height of the user's screen, making it hard to format output properly.
tldr.mechanism: Two new Telnet options were specified: NAOL (Negotiate About Output Line Width) and NAOP (Negotiate About Output Page Size), allowing the server to ask the client about its screen dimensions during connection.
tldr.outcome: Hosts could now discover and adapt to the user's terminal dimensions, making interactive sessions work better across different terminal types.

today: The Telnet protocol was used for remote terminal access for decades. These options became part of the Telnet standard, allowing better terminal handling. Modern systems now use SSH instead of Telnet for remote access.

sections.title: Two New Telnet Options Announced
sections.content:
This RFC announces the specification of two new Telnet options, the protocols that allow a Telnet client and server to negotiate capabilities during connection. The two options are NAOL (Negotiate About Output Line Width, NIC#20196) and NAOP (Negotiate About Output Page Size, NIC#20197).

These options were prepared by Dave Walden at BBN-NET and put online by Anita Coley and Dave Crocker at UCLA-NMC.
sections.eli5: Two new settings for the Telnet remote-login tool were documented and made official.

sections.title: Line Width and Page Size Options
sections.content:
The NAOL option (Negotiate About Output Line Width) allows a Telnet server to negotiate with the client (the user's terminal) to discover the maximum width of the display. This lets the host format output so lines do not wrap unexpectedly.

The NAOP option (Negotiate About Output Page Size) handles the vertical dimension, allowing the server to learn how many lines the user's terminal can display before it scrolls. This is useful for pagination and interactive screen formatting.
sections.eli5: NAOL lets computers talk about how wide a screen is. NAOP talks about how many lines tall it is.

sections.title: Terminal Negotiation During Connection
sections.content:
With these options, when a Telnet session begins, the server can use the Telnet option negotiation mechanism to ask the client for its display dimensions. Both the line width and page size become known to the host, which can then format interactive output—menus, forms, and line-wrapped text—to fit the user's actual terminal size.

This is especially important in the ARPANET era, when terminals vary widely in their capabilities and users might be connecting from many different terminal types over the network.
sections.eli5: When you log in via Telnet, the host computer can now ask your terminal 'how wide are you?' and 'how tall are you?' and adjust what it sends accordingly.
